assertion.name: Stage IV
assertion.description: Stage IV patients in the cited series had distant metastases at diagnosis. On NWTS-5, 7 of the 108 staged patients had stage IV disease; the lungs were the commonest metastatic site (3 patients), followed by bone (2), five of the seven relapsed, and five-year event-free survival for stage IV was 29%. On AREN0321 and AREN03B2, 7.6% of the 132 patients analysed had metastases (bone 20%, liver 20%, lung only 30%, lung and bone together 30%). AREN0321 added carboplatin for stage IV disease (regimen UH-1). The ten stage IV patients of the two studies combined had a four-year event-free survival of 58.3%, and the authors judge that they appeared to benefit from the carboplatin-containing regimen, although their outcomes remained unsatisfactory; the comparison is with the earlier NWTS-5 result rather than a concurrent control. On the SIOP 93-01 and SIOP 2001 trials, stage IV disease was a significant adverse prognostic factor for event-free survival.

assertion.name: Stage I
assertion.description: On the National Wilms Tumor Study-5 (NWTS-5), 12 of the 108 staged patients had stage I disease, and five-year event-free survival for stage I was 100%. On the Children's Oncology Group (COG) studies AREN0321 and AREN03B2, 10 of 132 patients (7.6%) were stage I, with a pooled four-year event-free survival of 90%. AREN0321 omitted radiotherapy for stage I disease when lymph nodes were sampled; none of the seven stage I patients treated without it had a local recurrence, and one stage I recurrence occurred in the brain. COG stage I rests on upfront nephrectomy and SIOP stage I on the tumour after preoperative chemotherapy, so a tumour that would be COG stage II or III if resected upfront could be SIOP stage I. The COG authors cite 39.5% of CCSK patients as stage I in the SIOP studies against 7.6% under COG staging, and suggest that stage I based on upfront nephrectomy is more favourable than stage I after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. On the SIOP 93-01 and SIOP 2001 trials, 2 of 80 stage I patients received radiotherapy.
assertion.notes: The SIOP 93-01 and SIOP 2001 report gives 42% of its 191 patients as stage I, and its radiotherapy figures count 80 stage I patients, whereas the COG report gives 39.5% (75 of 191) for the same studies. Neither cited text explains the difference.

selected_evidence.snippet: The seemingly superior outcomes for patients with stage I CCSK treated on the COG regimens suggests that stage I CCSK based on upfront nephrectomy is more favorable than stage I CCSK after neoadjuvant chemotherapy. This observation makes intuitive sense given that staging differences between COG and SIOP have resulted in COG selecting a very small and highly favorable subgroup of patients with CCSK for omission of RT. In the SIOP studies 39.5% (75/191) of patients with CCSK had stage I, compared to only 7.6% (10/132) in our study using COG staging. A patient who has a COG stage II or III tumor (if resected upfront) could have a SIOP stage I tumor after preoperative chemotherapy.

assertion.name: Stage III
assertion.description: On NWTS-5, 45 of the 108 staged patients had stage III disease, with five-year event-free and overall survival of 73% and 89%. NWTS-5 assessed prognostic factors, tumour spill among them, in its stage II and III patients together: no factor predicted overall survival on multivariate analysis, and only age of 12 months or more correlated with better event-free and overall survival on univariate analysis. On AREN0321 and AREN03B2, the 65 stage III patients had a pooled four-year event-free survival of 82.8%. Stage II and III patients on AREN0321 received regimen I with radiotherapy, all three local recurrences occurred in local stage III disease, and among local stage III tumours neither the initial procedure type, margin status nor lymph node involvement was prognostic. In a multicentre cohort of 54 children treated in Shanghai following NWTS strategies and staged by the NWTS system, five-year event-free survival was 71.1% for the 21 stage III patients. Across that cohort, inferior vena cava tumour thrombus (6 patients; event-free survival 41.7% against 87.4% without it) and tumour rupture before or during surgery (5 patients; 40% against 86.8%) were adverse factors on univariate analysis, and tumour rupture was the only independent adverse factor on multivariate analysis (HR 5.9, 95% CI 1.4 to 24.5). The authors attribute part of their stage III result to tumour rupture, with event-free survival of about 86% for stage III patients without it.

assertion.name: INRGSS Stage MS
assertion.description: Metastatic disease in a child younger than 18 months (547 days) with metastases confined to skin, liver and/or bone marrow, bone marrow involvement below 10% of nucleated cells, and meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scintigraphy negative in bone and bone marrow; the primary tumor may be L1 or L2, with no restriction on crossing or infiltrating the midline. INSS stage 4S is the narrower INSS counterpart, limited to infants younger than 12 months with an INSS stage 1 or 2 primary tumor and dissemination to liver, skin and/or bone marrow (under 10% involvement); the INRGSS extended the age limit to 18 months and admitted primaries infiltrating the midline (INSS stage 3). In an Italian series of 30 infants with stage IV-S disease treated in 1970-1981, the liver was the most frequent site of spread (87%), and subcutaneous nodules were recorded. In infants with stage IV-S or 4S disease the pattern is associated with spontaneous regression and good survival. In two infant cohorts, one limited to symptomatic or biologically unfavorable cases, most deaths occurred in infants younger than 2 months at diagnosis, most often from complications of hepatomegaly or extensive abdominal involvement. In the selected cohort, enrolled on the COG trial ANBL0531, no further deaths from hepatomegaly occurred after the protocol was amended to require immediate chemotherapy for infants younger than 2 months with evolving hepatomegaly. In a Children's Oncology Group cohort staged by the INRGSS, stage MS outcome was excellent except for MYCN-amplified tumors, which have a poor outcome. Whether toddlers aged 12 to 18 months with a 4S pattern of metastasis share the favorable outcome of infants is contested. In the INRG database, toddlers grouped by metastatic sites alone, without the marrow limit of stage MS, had worse event-free survival than infants with the 4S pattern and outcomes similar to stage 4 disease at the same age, and the authors concluded that tumor biology matters more than age or metastatic pattern. Registry data from two Japanese pediatric societies showed an excellent prognosis for stage 4s disease at 12 to 17 months.
assertion.notes: INSS stage 4S is recorded within this stage, not as a has_subtypes row, because the cancer granularity ladder (design decisions §3a) records stage under stages. The 4S category descends from the IV-S category of the 1971 Evans staging system, recognizing patients with metastatic disease limited to skin, liver and bone marrow who have superior outcomes, and the 1993 revision of the INSS added restrictions on age and bone marrow involvement for stage 4S. When the INRG Task Force extended the age limit to 18 months, it described the group aged 12 to 18 months as small, with an unclear outcome.
